title: Booting the Installation a Project Repository Declares
hints: A clone of a project repository is not an installation yet, and what it is missing is what the repository does not carry: the database, the files the storages point at, and everything below var/. typo3 setup is not what supplies them where the repository declares an import of its own: it refuses an existing config/system/settings.php with exception 1669747685, and a database that already holds tables with exception 1669747200. Where the environment declares a lifecycle, that lifecycle is the procedure rather than a description of one: typo3_project_describe reports the DDEV hooks and the pull recipes, and commands typed beside them boot something this repository does not describe.

An imported database was dumped from a different point in the history than the code in front of it, and typo3 extension:setup is what closes that gap. It migrates the schema of every active package before it runs each package's own setup, and it applies the additive suggestions only: add, change, create_table and change_table. Nothing is dropped and nothing is renamed, so a column the code no longer declares survives the run and no data is lost to it — and a table the code needs and the dump has not got is created. database:updateschema is not the core's command; a project whose hooks call it has typo3-console required beside the core.

Then the caches, because the dump carries them: the hash, pages and rootline caches are configured to the database backend by default, so the imported tables hold another installation's cached pages, hashes and rootlines. typo3 cache:flush empties them and the file-backed ones below var/cache with it; --group takes system, pages or di, and the default is all of them.

The backend users arrive with the dump and their passwords do not, so a boot creates one of its own. typo3 backend:user:create reads TYPO3_BE_USER_NAME, TYPO3_BE_USER_PASSWORD, TYPO3_BE_USER_EMAIL, TYPO3_BE_USER_GROUPS, TYPO3_BE_USER_ADMIN and TYPO3_BE_USER_MAINTAINER where the matching option is absent, and two of its answers only show up in a script. The password question is asked even under --no-interaction where neither the option nor the variable supplied one, so an unattended hook waits on stdin instead of failing. And a username the imported database already holds is refused with exception 1670797516, deleted rows counted — which is how a second boot fails on the step that worked the first time. backend:resetpassword is the way into a user that exists. Past those two checks the command reports nothing of its own: it hands the row to DataHandler, never reads that handler's errorLog, and exits 0 whatever came back — so the be_users row, or a login, is what says the user was created.

The site configuration is in the repository, so a clone is served under whatever host its base names. SiteMatcher builds one route per site and per language out of that base and puts its host, scheme and port on the route as requirements, so a request arriving on the local host matches no site: the result is a NullSite, and the installation answers its own root with No site configuration found. on an error page rather than with the page tree. page-not-found-within-a-site is the same reason line read for a request that did match a site, which is the half this one is told apart from. A base that is a bare path carries no host requirement and matches every host, and %env() in the base is the other way one configuration serves two environments. Above that sits the host check: VerifyHostHeader throws exception 1396795884 for an HTTP_HOST that does not match SYS/trustedHostsPattern, and an empty pattern denies every host there is.

Where the files are expected is in the database rather than in the repository. sys_file_storage carries basePath and pathType, and the local driver resolves a relative one below the public path and anything else as an absolute path — one outside the project root throws exception 1704807715, one that is not a directory throws exception 1299233097. So a dump brings the storage layout of the installation it came from, and a clone that imported the database and not the files keeps every sys_file row with nothing behind it. cleanup:localprocessedfiles is what deletes the processed-file records whose files are gone.

installation-setup is for an installation that has to be created rather than booted, and it is why an installer cannot read its own exit code: setup refuses an existing settings.php and a database that already holds tables, so that file is what an idempotent script tests for itself. project-configuration-files is who owns config/system/ while the environment generates into it, and taking additional.php over badly costs image processing, mail transport and the trusted hosts pattern the router's host name needs. project-build-and-scripts is what the repository does not commit, and it is why a scratch script does not go into the document root: it stays reachable over HTTP after the run that wrote it ends.

title: What a Failing Installation Writes Down and What It Only Displays
hints: An uncaught exception is written down as well as displayed, and the file is the copy an agent without a browser can read. The default LOG.writerConfiguration binds one FileWriter at warning with no options and the exception handler logs at critical, so the entry carries the exception's class, code, file, line and message — the same text the page shows, with the stack trace folded in where the debug handler wrote it. FileWriter derives its name rather than being given one: Environment::getVarPath() and then /log/typo3_<ten characters>.log, those characters an HMAC keyed with this installation's encryption key. So the name is not guessable and var/log/typo3_*.log is how the file is found; the var path is var/ at the project root of a Composer installation and public/typo3temp/var where there is no separate project root. An installation whose encryption key is still empty gets no default log file at all.

A log with nothing in it is an answer rather than a missing file, because some exceptions are displayed and never written down. AbstractExceptionHandler::writeLogEntries() returns before it writes anything — to the file and to sys_log alike — for a code in IGNORED_EXCEPTION_CODES or IGNORED_HMAC_EXCEPTION_CODES: the trusted-hosts exception 1396795884 first among them, then the two login rate limits, an unsupported HTTP method, a header with an invalid name or value, the IP and maintenance locks, and the HMAC validation failures. Those lists are constants of the core and no configuration reaches them. The first entry is what a clone served under an unexpected host throws, so the HTTP 500 a fresh installation is likeliest to answer with is exactly the one the log will not have.

What decides whether the page carries the message is SYS/displayErrors. At 1 the DebugExceptionHandler renders the message and the backtrace; at 0 the ProductionExceptionHandler renders "Oops, an error occurred!" and an empty message; at -1, which is the default, the request's remote address is matched against SYS/devIPmask — the loopback addresses until an environment widens it — and that picks between the two. The production page discloses the message in three cases only: exception 1396795884, a 40x client error, and a request an authenticated backend user made. The two halves therefore invert: the one exception production shows whatever happens is the one nothing logs, and a page saying only Oops means the log is the only copy of the rest.

A PHP fatal reaches none of this. SYS/errorHandlerErrors and SYS/exceptionalErrors both mask out E_ERROR, E_PARSE, E_COMPILE_ERROR and E_CORE_ERROR, so an exhausted memory limit or a syntax error is not turned into an exception and no exception handler sees it. It is in PHP's own error log, which belongs to the web server or the container rather than to the installation.

Two mechanisms produce most of what a fresh installation answers HTTP 500 and HTTP 404 with, and both are stated where the procedure is. installation-boot carries the trusted-hosts exception this log will not have, and the site base that matches no host — which throws nothing at all, so the reason line on the error page it answers the project root with is the only thing that failure wrote. page-not-found-within-a-site is where that line is read: it separates a request that matched no site from a page the matched site would not deliver, and both leave this log empty. project-configuration-files carries why the first request after a clone throws the trusted-hosts exception while the install command reported success.

title: Which Site Answers When Two Bases Collide
appliesTo: page not found at the site root
The requested page does not exist
backend works but the frontend does not
hints: TYPO3 matches a request against the routes of every site at once, and a base carrying a host beats a base that does not. SiteMatcher::getRouteCollectionForAllSites() builds one route per site and one per site language, and puts the base's host, scheme and port on each as requirements. A language base with no host of its own is prefixed with the site base, so the site's host reaches every one of its language routes. BestUrlMatcher then keeps every route whose path matched and orders them in sortMatchedRoutes(): each site's own entry route last, then the higher getHostMatchScore(), and the longer path match only after that. That score is 1 for a route that carried a host and matched it and 0 for one that carried none, so the host is compared before the path ever is.

So base: / is not a neutral default. It is the loser the moment another site names the host: a site on / or on /probe loses to a site on https://example.com/ even where its own path is the more specific one, and the request is answered out of that other site's page tree. A bare path therefore works only while it is the only site, and a second site under one host carries that host in its base as well.

The HTTP 404 this produces reads like a slug problem. The site that won answers whether or not it can serve the path, and one whose root page was deleted has nothing to serve — the site is unaffected by that, because it exists as long as its config.yaml declares a rootPageId above 0 and the pages table is never consulted for it. What comes back is "The requested page does not exist", the same sentence a mistyped slug produces. page-not-found-within-a-site reads that message for a request the right site answered, and the exclamation mark it turns on is the discriminator. Neither says which site answered, and typo3_project_describe is what lists every site with its base and its root page id.

installation-boot is the same matcher in the other direction, and reaching for it first costs the diagnosis: it is about a base naming a host nobody is on, where the request matches no site at all and gets a NullSite instead of the wrong site's page tree. initial-content-references is the third way a not-found at the root arrives and belongs to an installation that was seeded from a distribution — the imported site configuration lands on /<identifier>/, which is a base that is wrong rather than a base that lost. autogenerated-site-configuration is the fourth and is read off the identifier rather than off the symptom: a site nobody wrote, called autogenerated-<uid>-<md5 of that uid>, was written by the core when a page was created at the root, and its base is a sub-path of whatever URL the request that created it arrived on.

title: The Site the Core Writes for a New Root Page
appliesTo: site configuration I did not create
where did this site come from
where this site configuration came from
hints: A site configuration whose identifier appears in no file the repository ships was written by the core itself. TYPO3\CMS\Core\Hooks\CreateSiteConfiguration is a processDatamap_afterDatabaseOperations hook, and it fires when DataHandler inserts a new page with pid 0 or is_siteroot set, in the live workspace, in the default language and outside a version. The identifier it invents is autogenerated-<uid>-<md5 of that uid>, so a site named that way came from here and from nothing anybody wrote. A root page that already has a site is skipped, and a write that fails throws nothing: the SiteConfigurationWriteException is turned into a warning flash message, which leaves no site behind and nothing in a log to read.

The base it writes is why the installation then answers nothing at its own root. The hook cannot know the URL, so it takes the current request's site URL — the site path under CLI — and appends autogenerated-<uid>: a root page created from the backend gets a site answering under that sub-path and never under /. It then calls updateSlugForPage(), which runs a second DataHandler with an empty slug so the root page's slug regenerates. What createNewBasicSite() writes beside the base is one language — id 0, English, en_US.UTF-8, on base / — and empty errorHandling and routes, so the error pages and every further language are still to be configured by hand.

It fires for three page types only, held in a protected $allowedPageTypes: DOKTYPE_DEFAULT, DOKTYPE_LINK and DOKTYPE_SHORTCUT. A custom root page doktype therefore gets no site from the core, and an extension that wants one subclasses the hook to extend that array. The registration is $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['SC_OPTIONS']['t3lib/class.t3lib_tcemain.php']['processDatamapClass'], which DataHandler reads as a list of class names to instantiate, and core registers its own class under its own class name as the key. So an extension assigning that same key replaces core's hook rather than adding a second one, and ext_localconf.php is where a site that appeared for a page type the core does not list is read off.

initial-content-references is what this is mistaken for, and the hook draws the line itself: it returns early while DataHandler is importing, so a site that arrived with an import was never written here. The two are told apart by what they left — autogenerated-<uid>-<md5> on <site url>/autogenerated-<uid> from the hook, the package's own identifier on /<identifier>/ from the import — and neither is a slug problem. site-base-collision is the third and is what correcting this base runs into: written from a backend request the base carries that host, written under CLI it is a bare path, and a bare path loses every request to a site that names the host. Correct base in config/sites/<identifier>/config.yaml where this site is to answer at the root, and read what the installation actually has with typo3_project_describe.

title: What a Not-Found Means When the Site Was Matched
appliesTo: the requested page does not exist!
hints: A site answered, so the site configuration is settled and what is left is the page under it. The reason line on the error page is what says which of them it was. The requested page does not exist is the router finding nothing under that path, and the same sentence with an exclamation mark is a page it found and then withheld. ID was not an accessible page is an HTTP 403 for a page whose fe_group the visitor is not in, which frontend-access-restriction owns, and Page is not available in the requested language. is the translation rather than the page. A request that matched no site at all reads No site configuration found. in the same place, and that is what separates it from all four before anything else is read — installation-boot owns that case.

The line is there while the site configures no errorHandling for the status code: the core renders an error page of its own and appends Reason: <the message> to it. Accept: application/json reduces that page to {"reason": "..."}, which is the discriminator without the document around it. A site that does configure a handler for the code answers with the configured page and drops the message, so the reading is done before that is set up or from the page record itself. None of these is thrown, so the empty log installation-exception-output describes is what they produce rather than a second failure.

A hidden page is routed and then withheld, which is why its URL is right and its answer is a not-found. PageSlugCandidateProvider queries pages under the deleted and workspace restrictions alone, so the slug of a hidden page resolves like any other. The frontend then asks PageRepository::getPage() with the enable fields, gets nothing, reads the row again with getPage_noCheck(), and answers The requested page does not exist! where the disabled field is set. A logged-in backend user passes that check, so a page that renders in the browser you are logged into and answers not-found in a private window is hidden and nothing else.

How far up the tree that reaches is the rootline's answer, and hidden and deleted are opposites in it. RootlineUtility applies the deleted restriction alone, so a hidden page is still a rootline entry: a hidden root page answers its own URL with a not-found and takes nothing below it with it, unless it carries extendToSubpages — the inherited restriction frontend-access-restriction owns, which answers Subsection was found and not accessible instead. A deleted root page breaks the rootline of every page under it, so SiteFinder::getSiteByPageId() finds no site for any of them and the router drops them all as candidates. The whole tree then answers the sentence without the exclamation mark, while the site itself is untouched and the backend still shows the pages.

A page that is visible and still refused is its doktype: a spacer and a folder answer The requested page does not exist! as well, so that sentence covers the hidden page and the page type the frontend does not render alike, and the record is what tells the two apart. A whole tree that is hidden rather than only its root was written that way, and datahandler-seeding is the mechanism: pages.hidden defaults to 1 in TCA against 0 in the schema, so a page tree seeded by a script without saying otherwise arrives hidden and an export ships it as it is. Which of two sites answered is the question before this one, and site-base-collision owns it.

title: How a TYPO3 Project Repository Is Laid Out
hints: A project has two units and the answers differ per unit. The extension is a package: it can be required, tested and shipped on its own, and everything that is only true of it lives inside it. The repository around it is what gets deployed — the installation's configuration, the build tooling, the suites that need a running site. The core is the reference for the first one and no reference at all for the second, because the core is not a project. This is the layout of a repository that holds an installation; a repository that is only the extension has one unit and its own hint.

Which unit something belongs to has a test: could the extension still be installed into a different project and be tested there? Everything that survives that question belongs in the extension. So the PHP tests do — a functional test builds its own instance per test class and exercises the extension — and their phpunit configurations with them, because a suite whose configuration lives one repository up cannot run anywhere else. How that harness is assembled is the project extension tests hint.

The browser tests are the other half and belong to the repository. They run against the site as it is served, with its content, its site configuration and its built assets — that is a property of this installation, not of the extension. Merging the two costs the extension its independence and gains nothing: the two suites do not share a single fixture.
What goes around the site rather than in it is project-build-and-scripts, and what the installation is configured by is project-configuration-files.

title: Build/, the Scripts, and What Is Not Deployed
hints: Build/ at the project root is for what runs before or around the site rather than in it: the Playwright configuration and its specs, the static analysis configuration, a one-off script that seeds an installation. None of it is deployed, none of it belongs to a package, and keeping it in one directory is what keeps the root readable.

How anything is run is answered by the scripts in composer.json and package.json, and nowhere else — there is no runTests.sh here, and a colleague or an agent reads exactly those. Name them after what they do rather than after the tool behind them (test:unit, test:functional, test:e2e, with test running what needs nothing external), so the entry point survives the tool being replaced. typo3_project_describe reads them back.

A declared script is run as `ddev composer <name>` where the repository configures a DDEV project, and that form loses what a failing run wrote: a script exiting non-zero gives the caller exit code 1, no stdout at all, and its stderr folded into ddev's own error line. `ddev exec composer <name>` gives the script's own exit code and both streams whole, which is what a check whose finding is on stdout has to be run as — a formatter's diff, an analyser's report. The wrapper is still the form for anything that writes composer.json or vendor/, because keeping the host tree in step with the container is what it is for.

A suite that needs a database or a base URL takes it from the environment, with the defaults in the configuration file itself. Then a checkout runs the suite with no setup, and CI overrides the four or five variables it has to — the alternative is a file everyone edits and nobody commits.

var/ is TYPO3's writable state — caches, logs, sessions, and var/transient/ for what a temporary file is written to — and is not committed. A script that exists for one run therefore does not go there because it is ignored; it goes into Build/ with the rest of the tooling, or it is not kept at all.

The document root is the other place it does not go, and for the opposite reason: it is served. In a Composer installation it is the directory extra.typo3/cms.web-dir names in the root composer.json, public/ where that key is absent, and it is where the installer writes index.php. A DDEV project mounts the project directory at /var/www/html in the web container and serves the docroot below it, so /var/www/html/public is the document root of a TYPO3 project configured that way and /var/www/html is the project root above it. A debug or scratch script written into the document root is reachable over HTTP by anyone who can reach the site, for as long as it is there — and it is there after the run that wrote it ends, because nothing cleans it up. A file dropped at the project root instead is not served, but it outlives the run in the same way and is in the tree that gets deployed. Both are the same answer as var/: it goes into Build/, or it is not written at all.

Whether the built frontend assets are committed is a decision, not a rule, and it has to be made once and written down: committed, a deploy needs no Node and the diff carries generated files; not committed, the build has to run somewhere on the way to production. Both are normal, and the .gitignore is where the answer is read off.

What a Composer installation generates is written after that file is, so it is listed here rather than looked at. composer install puts index.php into the document root and publishes every installed package's Resources/Public below _assets/<hash>/, with vendor/ beside them at the project root. Setting the installation up adds the rest, through the folder structure the install tool fixes: the document root's .htaccess — web.config under IIS — and typo3temp/ with its assets/ below it, fileadmin/ with an .htaccess and _temp_/ and user_upload/ of its own, and var/ at the project root with an .htaccess of its own. A local file storage then writes _processed_/ inside itself as it processes an image, so fileadmin/_processed_/ arrives with the first thumbnail a page renders.

hints.text: The backend and the install tool have entry points of their own, so the document root also holds a typo3/ directory carrying typo3/index.php and typo3/install.php.

_assets_install/ sits beside _assets/ and is the same publishing done from the failsafe container, so it holds the packages the install tool boots and not the rest. Nothing writes a typo3/ directory any more: the backend and the install tool are reached through index.php, and no entry point is generated beside it.

hints: So the ignore file denies both directories and names back what the project owns, which is what typo3/cms-base-distribution ships: /vendor, /var/* with !/var/labels for the translations a language update downloads, and /public/* with !/public/.htaccess. Denying and naming back survives what enumerating does not — the set above moves between majors, and the file is written before the install that would show it. The .htaccess is the exception because the fixer writes it once: it creates the file where none exists and leaves the content of one that does, so the rewrite rules a project adds to it are the project's to keep. A sitepackage or fileadmin content that has to be committed is named back the same way.

title: What the Installation Is Configured By
hints: The installation's own site configuration is config/sites/<identifier>/config.yaml at the project root, which is where TYPO3 reads it from. What a sitepackage ships in Initialisation/Site/<identifier>/ is a seed for an installation that has none yet, not the same file: editing the shipped copy changes nothing here, and editing this one ships nothing.

The two files in config/system/ have different owners. settings.php is the configuration array written by TYPO3's setup and configuration tools. additional.php is optional PHP loaded afterwards, so it is the project-owned place for environment-dependent overrides such as database credentials, encryption keys, trusted hosts and mail transport. Keep that code in version control and document the environment variables it consumes; do not hand-edit generated values into settings.php. Neither file on its own is the effective value, because additional.php is loaded after settings.php and writes over it. typo3_configuration_lookup with the path answers what the installation resolved, SYS/trustedHostsPattern for the host check.

A TYPO3 project type makes DDEV contest that boundary: DDEV generates config/system/additional.php and owns any settings file that still contains #ddev-generated. It writes four sections, merged over $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS'] with array_replace_recursive behind IS_DDEV_PROJECT: DB for its own database container, GFX for the ImageMagick in that container, MAIL for its mail catcher, and SYS with trustedHostsPattern, devIPmask and displayErrors. Remove that marker to take the file over, or disable DDEV settings management; DDEV then leaves an existing user-managed additional.php untouched. Taking it over means supplying the three non-database sections too: a replacement that writes only the database settings back loses image processing and mail transport, and drops the trusted hosts pattern, without which TYPO3 rejects the host name the DDEV router forwards. Treat config/system/.gitignore the same way. If DDEV still owns both, a regeneration can overwrite additional.php while restoring an /additional.php ignore entry; when the project file has not yet been committed, that hides its loss from ordinary git status. After a DDEV configuration change, inspect both files and verify additional.php is still tracked before committing.

When DDEV writes that file is decided by detection rather than by the start. It chooses the settings paths on every start by looking for an installed TYPO3 — vendor/typo3/cms-core/Classes/Information/Typo3Version.php in a Composer installation, docroot/typo3 in a legacy one — and finding neither it points both paths at the project root and writes nothing there, config/system/.gitignore included. So the first ddev start in a clone whose dependencies are not installed leaves no additional.php, and every request then fails with exception 1396795884 for the trusted hosts pattern that file supplies, while typo3 setup reports success because it writes settings.php from the environment variables. That detection also runs before the post-start hooks, so a hook that installs the dependencies gets the file written at the next start rather than in that one. A boot that starts the environment before Composer therefore starts it again afterwards, and that second start ends the ordering for good. Committing a project-owned additional.php is the other way out rather than the first: it is there from the first request, and it puts installation state under version control. A repository that deploys from the checkout already carries that state. An extension repository does not — the Composer root is the package there and config/ is ignored whole, which extension-repository-installation states.

DDEV is a local-development environment, not the production configuration source. Keep a DDEV-managed additional.php generated and ignored where the four generated sections are all the local environment needs. That generator knows only DDEV's own database container — mysqli or pdo_pgsql at host db — and has no variant that reads the driver the installation was set up with. So an installation on SQLite or with omit_containers: [db] cannot leave the file generated: the DB block merges over the connection settings.php carries and points it at a container that is not running. Take the file over there — remove the #ddev-generated line, drop the DB section, keep GFX, MAIL and SYS — since disabling settings management ends the same collision but leaves all three to be written by hand. When the repository owns one additional.php for every environment, read deployment values and secrets from environment variables and guard DDEV-only overrides with IS_DDEV_PROJECT; never commit production secrets.

title: Verifying a Change Against the Installation Rather Than Against Its Own Output
appliesTo: which language the code is in
hints: What a script printed is evidence that the print was reached. A guard that never matched, a regex that edited nothing and a variable the shell refused to assign all end in the same success line, so the state is read afterwards with something that had no part in producing it.
For a change to files, that reader is a search over the result rather than the script's own count: the count is of the list it iterated, and the two differ exactly when the edit failed.

For a change to records, it is a query against the installation's database — a group by over the column that changed, a count of the rows the old value is still on. The installation's own console at vendor/bin/typo3 and the backend are where those run, because that is where the permissions apply.

A green test suite is a claim about its assertions. It says nothing about rows the assertions never look at, and a suite that passed through a broken installation is the ordinary case rather than a surprising one.

For anything an editor sees, the reader is the backend itself: the page module draws "Invalid value" on a record whose type is one nothing declares, and the record list does not — no frontend page and no HTTP status says either.

Repair the class rather than the instance. A defect found in one file, one table or one row is a defect of the unit its cause is stated in, so the search that found it is run again for every sibling before the fix is reported — one TCA file out of five with the same option is the shape this takes.

A convention is a precondition on writing rather than a pass over what is written. A sweep corrects the files that exist and reaches nothing written afterwards, and it reports success either way — so before a new file of a kind is written, the question is what the existing files of that kind already do: which language their comments and messages are in, how they are named, what they import. That is one search over the repository and it is the half a linter does not check.
